opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest thing is to make it really cheap for the person inside the lab to help you. People at labs are often extremely busy, and they're also constrained in what they can say. So if you show up with a vague "what should I work on?", that's quite hard to answer well. If you show up with "here's a two-paragraph summary of my project, here are the three directions I'm considering, which seems most useful, and is there anything obviously wrong with my assumptions?", that's something someone can answer in ten minutes, and often will.

Second, be realistic about what they can share. Lab researchers often can't tell you about internal results, what techniques are being used in production, or what's on the roadmap. But they can usually tell you whether a direction seems important, whether something is already well understood internally so you'd be duplicating work, or whether your threat model matches how things actually work in practice. Those are some of the most valuable signals an external researcher can get, so ask questions they can answer without getting into trouble.

Third, I'd invest in relationships rather than one-off cold emails. Show up to conferences and workshops, post your work publicly, engage thoughtfully with things lab researchers have written. When someone has seen good work from you, they're much more likely to give you a careful answer, and much more likely to say "actually, you should talk to this person." Producing solid public work is probably the best networking strategy in this field.

Finally, take feedback seriously but not as gospel. People inside labs have a particular vantage point. They know a lot about frontier systems, but they can also have blind spots shaped by their organization's priorities. External researchers are valuable partly because they can work on things labs underrate. So use their input to calibrate, especially to avoid wasted effort, but keep your own judgment about what's important.

r001.rationale: The response says lab researchers are often busy but does not distinguish junior researchers from senior leaders or say juniors have more time.

r002.rationale: It mentions that lab researchers may refer someone to another person, but does not identify junior researchers as a route for escalating promising external research to senior researchers.

r003.rationale: The response recommends asking for input on a project, but does not clearly recommend dialogue throughout the research process rather than only after it is complete.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that people inside labs are often much more willing to help than external researchers expect, but you need to make it really easy for them. The core constraint is time and attention, not willingness. Someone at a lab might have ten minutes to spare, and the question is whether you can extract something useful from those ten minutes or whether you burn them on context-setting.

So concretely, a few things. One: come with specific, well-scoped questions rather than "what do you think of my research agenda?" Something like "I'm trying to decide between approach A and approach B for this problem, here's my one-paragraph reasoning, does this match your intuitions?" is dramatically easier to answer. The more work you've done upfront, the more valuable the response can be, and honestly the more likely you are to get one at all.

Two: write things up publicly, or at least in a shareable form. A lot of my most useful interactions with external researchers have come from someone posting a short write-up on LessWrong or the Alignment Forum or even just Twitter, and me or a colleague reading it and going "oh, that's interesting, but you've missed this thing." Public work is a much lower-friction way to get feedback than cold emails, because the person reading it can engage on their own schedule and with whatever depth they feel like. And it also builds a track record, which matters a lot. If I've seen three good posts from someone, I'm much more inclined to spend an hour on a call with them.

Three: ask for intuitions and taste, not secrets. People at labs mostly can't tell you about unpublished results or internal details, and asking puts them in an awkward position. But they absolutely can tell you "I think this direction is less promising than it looks because of X" or "the thing I'd be worried about with this experiment is Y." That kind of tacit knowledge about what's actually likely to work is, I think, the most valuable thing insiders have to offer, and it's almost entirely shareable.

And then four, which is a bit more meta: don't over-index on insider input. There's a tendency to treat lab researchers as oracles, and we're often wrong, and we have our own blind spots that come from being in a particular environment with particular incentives. Some of the best external work has come from people who were somewhat contrarian relative to the lab consensus. So use the input as one signal among many rather than deferring to it. The ideal is something like: get the insider's take, understand their reasoning, and then make your own call.

I'd also just say, mentorship programmes like MATS are genuinely one of the best channels for this, because they formalise the relationship. You get sustained access to someone rather than scattered ten-minute conversations, and that compounds a lot.

r002.rationale: It does not describe junior researchers as a way to bring promising external work to senior researchers.

r003.rationale: It suggests asking focused questions, including while choosing between approaches, but does not clearly recommend dialogue throughout the research process rather than only after completion.

astra-6.text:
I’d recommend making it really easy for someone to give you useful feedback. Rather than asking, “What should I work on?” come with a concrete proposal: “Here’s the question I’m trying to answer, here’s why I think it matters, and here’s the experiment I’m considering. Would this result actually be useful to you? Is there something obvious I’m missing?”

Ideally, do that before you’ve spent six months on the project. A short conversation early on can save you a lot of time, especially if there’s some practical constraint that makes your proposed approach less relevant than you think.

And I’d talk to a few different people. Someone inside a lab has a particular perspective, based on their team and what they work on; they’re not an oracle about what research matters. Treat their feedback as evidence that informs your judgment. The goal is to understand what would make your work useful, while still having your own reasons for doing it.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d recommend making it very easy for someone to give you useful feedback. Rather than asking, “What should I work on?” come with a concrete idea and a short explanation of why you think it matters. Then ask something specific, like, “What’s the biggest reason this might not be useful?” or “What result would make you interested in this?”

And ideally, do that before you’ve spent six months on the project. A quick conversation early on can expose an assumption you could otherwise spend a lot of time building on. You can then go away, do some work, and come back with something concrete.

I’d also talk to several people. Someone inside a lab has useful context, but they’re still one person with particular interests and blind spots. Treat their feedback as evidence to inform your judgement, rather than as a definitive verdict on whether your research is worthwhile.
